subject: geography

moments.title: Christaller's Central Place Theory
moments.body: Christaller publishes 'Die zentralen Orte in Süddeutschland', based on settlement patterns in southern Germany. He argues that towns of different sizes should be arranged in nested hexagonal hierarchies determined by three principles: market, transport and administration.
moments.takeaway: The theory predicts that lower-order centres (villages providing basic goods) cluster within the service areas of higher-order centres (regional towns).

moments.title: Christaller and the Nazi regime
moments.who: Walter Christaller working for the SS planning office
moments.body: Christaller joined the NSDAP in 1940 and worked on the Generalplan Ost — Nazi plans for reorganising occupied Eastern Europe along his central-place hierarchies, with massive ethnic cleansing. He left the party after the war and joined the Communist Party of Germany.
moments.takeaway: The theory's apparent value-neutrality enabled its use in genocidal planning. Geographer Trevor Barnes and others have documented this history.

now.title: Theory in practice
now.body:
Central Place Theory remains in A-level textbooks. Modern retail geography (catchment areas, gravity models) descends from it. Reilly's law of retail gravitation (1931) and Huff's probabilistic model (1964) are related.

Critics: it assumes isotropic plains with uniform consumers, ignores history, and underplays transport infrastructure. Real settlement patterns often reflect path dependence (rivers, historical roads) more than abstract geometry.
now.open_questions: Is the theory useful as a baseline against which to measure real patterns, or as a description of how cities should work? The first is defensible; the second has caused planning disasters.

reflection: Theoretical geography can be politically deployable. Christaller's hexagons are simultaneously a piece of mid-century systematic geography and a tool that was put to murderous use — both facts belong in the history of the discipline.
